items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Copious'.
items.explanation: Copious means existing in large quantities, so Abundant is the closest synonym. Scarce, Meagre, Limited and Sparse all suggest small quantities, the opposite sense.

items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Meticulous'.
items.explanation: Meticulous describes someone who pays great attention to detail, so Careful is the nearest meaning. Careless, Hasty, Rough and Negligent all suggest a lack of care.

items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Audacious'.
items.explanation: Audacious means showing a willingness to take bold risks, so Bold is the closest synonym. Timid, Cowardly, Shy and Cautious all describe the opposite attitude.

items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Ephemeral'.
items.explanation: Ephemeral means lasting for a very short time, so Short-lived is the nearest meaning. Eternal, Permanent, Lasting and Enduring all suggest long duration, the opposite sense.

items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Pragmatic'.
items.explanation: Pragmatic means dealing with problems in a practical rather than theoretical way, so Practical is the closest synonym. Idealistic, Theoretical, Unrealistic and Romantic all point away from practicality.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Opaque'.
items.explanation: Opaque means not allowing light to pass through, so Transparent is its direct opposite. Cloudy, Dark, Murky and Dense are all close in sense to opaque.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Reluctant'.
items.explanation: Reluctant means unwilling or hesitant to do something, so Willing is its opposite. Unwilling, Hesitant, Loath and Averse all express the same reluctance.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Frugal'.
items.explanation: Frugal means careful with money and avoiding waste, so Extravagant is its opposite. Thrifty, Economical, Sparing and Saving are all synonyms of frugal.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Benevolent'.
items.explanation: Benevolent means kind and generous towards others, so Malevolent, meaning wishing harm to others, is its opposite. Kind, Generous, Charitable and Humane all share the benevolent sense.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Diligent'.
items.explanation: Diligent means showing steady hard work and care, so Lazy is its opposite. Industrious, Hardworking, Assiduous and Sedulous are all synonyms of diligent.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to bite the dust'.
items.explanation: To bite the dust means to fail or to be defeated, as in a contest or an endeavour. The other options take the words literally and miss the figurative sense.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to burn the midnight oil'.
options: To work late into the night
items.explanation: To burn the midnight oil means to work or study late into the night. The idiom comes from the days of oil lamps, and the other options miss that figurative sense.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'a blessing in disguise'.
options: A lucky accident with no cost
A good thing that seemed bad at first
items.explanation: A blessing in disguise is something that seems bad or unlucky at first but turns out to be good. The other options either take the words literally or describe a different idea.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to hit the nail on the head'.
options: To say exactly the right thing
items.explanation: To hit the nail on the head means to say or do exactly the right thing, describing a remark precisely. The other options take the carpentry image literally.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to let the cat out of the bag'.
items.explanation: To let the cat out of the bag means to reveal a secret, usually by accident. The other options take the words literally and miss the figurative meaning.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: The seeds are sown just before the first rains arrive. B: By September the fields turn a deep green. C: In the villages of Vidarbha, farming follows the rhythm of the monsoon. D: If the rains fail, the crop fails with them.
items.explanation: The paragraph must open with the general statement about farming and the monsoon, then move to sowing, then to growth, and end with the consequence of failed rain. That order is C, A, B, D.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: Gutenberg's press used movable metal type, which could be rearranged for each page. B: Before the printing press, books were copied by hand, a slow and costly process. C: Within fifty years, printed books had spread across Europe. D: The press made books cheaper, and cheaper books reached far more readers.
items.explanation: The paragraph opens with the situation before printing, then introduces Gutenberg's press, then gives its effect on price and readers, and closes with the spread across Europe. That order is B, A, D, C.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: The first line will run for twenty-two kilometres through the heart of the city. B: Construction began in 2019, and the tunnelling alone took three years. C: The city council approved the metro project after a decade of debate. D: When it opens, the metro is expected to carry four lakh passengers a day.
items.explanation: The paragraph must start with the approval of the project, then describe construction, then give the scale of the first line, and end with the expected ridership. That order is C, B, A, D.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: The vapour cools, condenses and falls back as rain. B: Heat from the sun turns water from seas and lakes into vapour. C: Part of the rain flows into rivers, and part seeps into the ground. D: The cycle then begins again, endlessly repeating itself.
items.explanation: The water cycle starts with evaporation by the sun's heat, then condensation and rain, then the fate of the fallen rain, and closes with the repetition of the cycle. That order is B, A, C, D.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: She began by listing every topic and the marks it carried. B: Two weeks before the examination, Meera finally made a study plan. C: She then gave the weakest topics the most hours. D: By the last day she had revised each topic twice.
items.explanation: The paragraph opens with Meera making the plan, then listing topics, then allocating the most hours to weak topics, and ends with the result of the revision. That order is B, A, C, D.

items.question: Choose the word that best fits the blank. The committee's decision was so ______ that even its own members could not explain it.
items.explanation: Arbitrary fits because a decision that even its own members cannot explain was made without reason or principle. Transparent, predictable, generous and timely all contradict that sense.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Choose the word that best fits the blank. The old bridge, ______ by floods every year, was finally rebuilt on higher pillars.
items.explanation: Damaged fits because floods harm a bridge, and the rebuilding follows from that harm. Ignored, painted, celebrated and guarded give no reason for rebuilding on higher pillars.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Choose the pair of words that best fits the blanks. The manager's ______ tone ______ the junior staff, who had expected praise for their work.
items.explanation: Harsh and disheartened fit together because a harsh tone would upset staff who expected praise. The other pairs describe positive tones that would please rather than dishearten the staff.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Choose the word that best fits the blank. Despite years of research, scientists still ______ why some patients recover far faster than others.
items.explanation: Do not fully understand fits because the sentence says the question is still open despite years of research. Understand fully, have proven and can predict exactly all contradict that, and have forgotten makes no sense.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Choose the pair of words that best fits the blanks. A good leader ______ criticism with grace and ______ it into better decisions.
items.explanation: Accepts and turns fit because a good leader takes criticism well and uses it constructively. The other pairs describe avoiding or wasting criticism, which is the opposite of good leadership.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) Neither of the two / (b) brothers are / (c) willing to sell / (d) the ancestral house.
items.explanation: Neither is singular, so the verb must be is, not are. The error is in part (b). The other parts are grammatically correct.

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) The committee / (b) have decided / (c) to postpone / (d) the meeting by a week.
items.explanation: Committee is a collective noun used here as a single body, so the verb must be has, not have. The error is in part (b).

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) She is / (b) one of the best / (c) players who / (d) has represented the state.
items.explanation: The relative clause refers to players, a plural noun, so the verb must be have, not has. The error is in part (d).

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) The train arrived / (b) at the station / (c) more earlier / (d) than expected.
items.explanation: Earlier is already comparative, so more earlier is a double comparative and wrong. The error is in part (c); the correct form is simply earlier.

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) Each of the students / (b) have submitted / (c) their assignments / (d) on time.
items.explanation: Each is singular, so the verb must be has, not have. The error is in part (b). Their is accepted as a gender-neutral plural pronoun for each student.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. The new policy, which was introduced last month, have already changed the way the office works.
items.explanation: Policy is singular, so the verb must be has, not have. The correct replacement is has already changed. The other options keep the agreement error or introduce a new one.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. Neither the workers nor the manager was aware of the change in the schedule.
items.explanation: With neither nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, manager, which is singular, so was is correct. The sentence as written is correct, so no correction is required.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. The book, along with the notes, were left on the table.
items.explanation: The subject is the book, which is singular; along with the notes does not make it plural. The verb must be was left, so the correct replacement is was left.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. He is the most intelligent of the two brothers.
items.explanation: When comparing two people or things, the comparative form is used, so most intelligent must become more intelligent. The other options keep the error or are ungrammatical.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. By the time the guests arrived, the dinner had been served already.
items.explanation: The past perfect had been served is correct here because the serving happened before the guests arrived in the past. The sentence as written is correct, so no correction is required.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: One of my friends are a doctor.
One of my friends is doctors.
One of my friend is a doctor.
One of my friends is a doctor.
One of my friends are doctors.
items.explanation: One is singular, so the verb must be is, and friends must be plural after one of. Only the second sentence satisfies both rules.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The data shows a clear trend.
The datas shows a clear trend.
The data show a clear trend.
The data showing a clear trend.
The data are shows a clear trend.
items.explanation: Data is a plural noun in formal usage, so it takes the plural verb show. Only the third sentence is correct; the first uses a singular verb with a plural noun.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Neither the students nor the teacher were present.
Neither the teacher nor the students was present.
Neither the teacher nor the students were present.
Neither the students nor the teacher was presents.
Neither the teachers nor the student were present.
items.explanation: With neither nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, students, which is plural, so were is correct. Only the third sentence follows the proximity rule correctly.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: She did not hardly finish the work.
She hardly did finish the work.
She did hardly finish the work.
She did not finish hardly the work.
items.explanation: Hardly is itself negative, so it must not be combined with not. The fourth sentence uses hardly correctly with a positive verb.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The sceneries of Kashmir are beautiful.
The scenery of Kashmir are beautiful.
The sceneries of Kashmir is beautiful.
The scenery of Kashmir is beautiful.
The sceneries of Kashmir have beautiful.
items.explanation: Scenery is an uncountable noun with no plural form, and it takes a singular verb. Only the second sentence is correct.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'One who can use both hands equally well'.
items.explanation: Ambidextrous describes a person equally skilled with both hands. Ambivalent means having mixed feelings, Ambiguous means unclear, Amphibian is an animal, and Amateur is a non-professional.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'A person who speaks many languages'.
items.explanation: Polyglot is a person who knows and uses several languages. Bilingual means two languages only, Linguist studies language, Orator is a public speaker, and Translator converts between languages.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'An extreme fear of heights'.
items.explanation: Acrophobia is the fear of heights. Claustrophobia is fear of closed spaces, Agoraphobia is fear of open or crowded places, Hydrophobia is fear of water, and Nyctophobia is fear of darkness.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'One who hates mankind'.
items.explanation: Misanthrope is a person who dislikes or hates humankind. Philanthropist and Altruist love or help others, Misogynist hates women specifically, and Egotist is self-centred.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'A place where birds are kept'.
items.explanation: Aviary is a large enclosure for keeping birds. Aquarium is for fish, Apiary is for bees, Stable is for horses, and Kennel is for dogs.

items.question: Book is to Read as Pen is to:
items.explanation: A book is the object used for reading, just as a pen is the object used for writing. Draw uses a pencil or brush rather than a pen in this pairing, and Ink, Paper and Hold are not the matching activity.

items.question: Doctor is to Hospital as Teacher is to:
items.explanation: A doctor works in a hospital, just as a teacher works in a school. Student, Book, Class and Lesson are things a teacher deals with, not the place of work.

items.question: Ocean is to Water as Desert is to:
items.explanation: An ocean is a large body of water, just as a desert is a large expanse of sand. Heat and Dryness describe the desert but are not its substance, while Camel and Oasis are found in it.

items.question: Courage is to Fear as Honesty is to:
items.explanation: Courage is the opposite of fear, just as honesty is the opposite of deceit. Truth is a synonym of honesty rather than its opposite, and Virtue and Morality are broader categories.

items.question: Spider is to Web as Bird is to:
items.explanation: A spider builds a web as its home, just as a bird builds a nest. Feather, Wing and Egg are parts of a bird, and Sky is where it flies, not what it builds.

items.passage: In less than a decade, India has moved from a cash-heavy economy to one of the world's most active digital payment markets. The Unified Payments Interface, launched in 2016, now processes more than ten billion transactions a month, a scale no other real-time payment system has reached. A vegetable vendor in a small town and a shopkeeper in a metro city both display the same square QR code, and a customer with any bank account can pay either of them in seconds, free of charge. This simplicity is the core of the system's success. Unlike card networks, which charge merchants a fee on every sale, UPI transfers cost the merchant nothing, so even the smallest seller has a reason to accept them. The government pushed the change further by linking bank accounts to mobile numbers and identity numbers, bringing crores of first-time account holders into the formal financial system. For these new users, a payment app became the first banking service they ever used, and for many it remains the only one. The benefits are visible. Small businesses that once kept all their money in cash now have a record of every sale, and that record helps them borrow from banks at lower rates. Wages that used to be paid in envelopes on a Friday evening now arrive directly into workers' accounts, on time and in full. Street vendors report that digital payments have also cut the risk of carrying cash home late at night, and many now save a part of each day's earnings through the same app that collects their payments. The National Payments Corporation, which runs UPI, has kept the system open so that any bank or app can join it, and that openness is a large part of why adoption spread so quickly. Government subsidies for cooking gas and food reach beneficiaries without passing through layers of middlemen who once took a cut. Yet the shift is far from complete. Surveys show that cash still accounts for a large share of everyday transactions, especially in rural areas where mobile networks are weak and smartphones are shared within families. Trust is another barrier. Stories of fraud, a wrong tap that sends money to a stranger, or a failed transaction that takes days to reverse make cautious users fall back on cash. Digital literacy programmes have helped, but they reach only a fraction of the people who need them, and older users in particular need patient, repeated guidance. The next stage of the journey will be harder than the first. Growth so far came from urban users with good phones and good connectivity. Reaching the remaining users means solving harder problems: patchy networks, low literacy, fear of fraud, and the simple habit of cash built over generations. Banks and payment companies are responding with voice-based payments in local languages, offline modes that work without internet, and faster grievance redressal for failed transactions. Whether these efforts succeed will decide if digital payments become truly universal or remain a convenience for the already connected. The lesson of the last decade is that technology alone does not change behaviour; it is the combination of free access, simple design, and trust that moves people from cash to code.
items.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Digital payments in India have grown fast but still face challenges in trust and inclusion
Smartphones are the main reason for India's economic growth
Cash payments are better than digital payments in rural India
UPI is the only payment system used in India
The government should ban cash transactions
items.explanation: The passage traces the rapid growth of digital payments and then turns to the barriers that remain, so the first option captures its full arc. The other options are either too narrow or contradict the passage.

items.question: According to the passage, why do small sellers accept UPI payments?
options: Because the government forces them to accept UPI
Because UPI transfers cost the merchant nothing
Because customers refuse to pay in cash
Because banks pay sellers a bonus for each UPI sale
Because card networks charge very high fees to customers
items.explanation: The passage states that unlike card networks, which charge merchants a fee, UPI transfers cost the merchant nothing, giving even the smallest seller a reason to accept them.

items.question: How have digital payment records helped small businesses, as per the passage?
options: They have removed the need for bank accounts
They have helped businesses borrow from banks at lower rates
They have made all sales tax free
They have doubled the number of customers
They have removed the need to keep any accounts
items.explanation: The passage says a record of every sale helps small businesses borrow from banks at lower rates. The other options are not stated anywhere in the passage.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a barrier to digital payments?
options: Weak mobile networks in rural areas
Fear of fraud and failed transactions
Low digital literacy among older users
High charges on UPI transfers for customers
The habit of using cash built over generations
items.explanation: The passage lists weak networks, fear of fraud, low literacy and the habit of cash as barriers, but it stresses that UPI is free for users and merchants, so high charges are not mentioned as a barrier.

items.question: What does the author mean by saying technology alone does not change behaviour?
options: Technology has no role in payment systems
People change habits only when access is free, design is simple, and trust exists
Cash will always remain the main mode of payment
The government should stop promoting digital payments
Smartphones are too expensive for most Indians
items.explanation: The closing lines say it is the combination of free access, simple design and trust that moves people from cash to code, which is exactly what the second option states.

items.question: According to the passage, what happens to government subsidies when paid digitally?
options: They reach beneficiaries without middlemen taking a cut
They are delayed by several weeks
They are paid only to urban beneficiaries
They require a smartphone for every family member
They are converted into cash at the bank
items.explanation: The passage says subsidies for cooking gas and food reach beneficiaries without passing through layers of middlemen who once took a cut.

items.question: Which of the following best describes the tone of the passage?
items.explanation: The author presents both the achievements and the remaining problems of digital payments with evidence, which is a balanced and analytical tone rather than angry, humorous, technical or pessimistic.

items.question: What is the author most likely to agree with?
options: Digital payments will soon replace cash completely without further effort
Voice-based payments and offline modes are needed to reach the remaining users
Rural users should be forced to stop using cash
Card networks are better than UPI for small sellers
Digital literacy programmes have already solved the trust problem
items.explanation: The passage says banks are responding with voice-based payments, offline modes and faster grievance redressal to reach remaining users, and the author presents these as the way forward.

items.passage: In a cold stone parsonage on the Yorkshire moors, three sisters wrote novels that would outlive them by nearly two centuries. Charlotte, Emily and Anne Bronte lived far from the literary world of London, yet their books reached straight into its heart. When Charlotte's Jane Eyre appeared in 1847, readers were startled by a heroine who was plain, poor and fiercely independent, and who demanded to be loved for her mind rather than her face. In the same year, Emily's Wuthering Heights shocked readers even more with its wild landscapes and its furious, unsentimental love. Anne's quieter novels, Agnes Grey and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, attacked the drinking and cruelty of idle gentlemen with a moral clarity her sisters did not attempt. What made the sisters remarkable was not only what they wrote but how they wrote it. They had spent their childhood inventing imaginary kingdoms, writing tiny hand-sewn books filled with stories of heroes, villains and wars. That private world of invention gave them a freedom that formal education might have taken away, and their novels carry the same intensity of a child's secret game played with adult seriousness. Their isolation mattered too. The moors around Haworth were empty and harsh, and the sisters walked them daily in all weathers. The landscape entered their fiction directly: the wind, the heather, the stone walls and the sudden storms became characters in their own right, shaping the moods of the people who lived among them. Yet the sisters were not cut off from ideas. They read widely, followed the newspapers, and argued about politics and religion at the dinner table. Their novels engage with the great questions of their age: the position of women, the cruelty of the class system, and the right of the individual to judge for herself. Jane Eyre's famous declaration that women feel just as men feel was a direct challenge to a society that expected women to be silent and obedient. The sisters paid a price for their honesty. Critics called their work coarse and unfeminine, and they published under male pen names to be taken seriously. Charlotte wrote as Currer Bell, Emily as Ellis Bell, and Anne as Acton Bell, and the secret of their identity held for years. Their lives were short: Emily died at thirty, Anne at twenty-nine, and Charlotte at thirty-eight, yet in that brief span they changed the English novel for ever. Charlotte lived long enough to see her work praised and to meet the writers she admired, but she outlived both her sisters and mourned them for the rest of her short life. Later writers learned from them that a novel could be built around a woman's inner life, that landscape could carry emotion, and that passion need not be polite to be true. Today the parsonage at Haworth is a museum, and visitors still walk the moors the sisters walked, looking for the places their fiction made famous. The books remain in print in dozens of languages, read by people who have never seen Yorkshire and never will, because the feelings in them belong to no single place or time.
items.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The Bronte sisters changed the English novel through their intense, original fiction
The Yorkshire moors are the most beautiful place in England
Charlotte Bronte was a better writer than her sisters
Novels in the 1840s were mostly written by men
The Bronte sisters were famous during their lifetimes
items.explanation: The passage describes how the three sisters wrote original novels that changed the English novel, covering their themes, their isolation and their lasting influence, which the first option sums up.

items.question: According to the passage, what startled readers about Jane Eyre?
options: Its heroine was plain, poor and fiercely independent
It was written in a foreign language
It was the longest novel of its time
Its author was a man from London
It had no plot at all
items.explanation: The passage says readers were startled by a heroine who was plain, poor and fiercely independent and demanded to be loved for her mind rather than her face.

items.question: What did the sisters' childhood games contribute to their writing?
options: They taught them to write in tiny handwriting
They gave them a freedom and intensity that shaped their novels
They made them want to write only for children
They kept them away from books and reading
They made their novels light and humorous
items.explanation: The passage says their childhood invention of imaginary kingdoms gave them a freedom formal education might have taken away, and their novels carry that same intensity.

items.question: How did the Yorkshire landscape affect the sisters' fiction?
options: It made their novels boring and repetitive
It became a living presence that shaped the moods of their characters
It prevented them from writing about cities
It made them write only about nature
It had no effect on their writing at all
items.explanation: The passage says the wind, heather, stone walls and storms became characters in their own right, shaping the moods of the people who lived among them.

items.question: Why did the sisters publish under male pen names?
options: Because women were not allowed to write novels
Because they wanted to hide from their father
Because critics called their work coarse and unfeminine, and they wanted to be taken seriously
Because their real names were too long
Because the publisher insisted on it
items.explanation: The passage states that critics called their work coarse and unfeminine, and they published under male pen names to be taken seriously.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Emily Bronte died at the age of thirty
Anne Bronte wrote The Tenant of Wildfell Hall
The sisters lived in a parsonage at Haworth
Charlotte Bronte lived longer than her sisters
The sisters never read newspapers or followed politics
items.explanation: The passage says they read widely, followed newspapers and argued about politics, so the last statement is false. The other four statements are all given in the passage.

items.question: What did later writers learn from the Bronte sisters, as per the passage?
options: That novels should always be set in Yorkshire
That a novel could be built around a woman's inner life and landscape could carry emotion
That writers should always use pen names
That novels must be polite to succeed
That only short lives produce great books
items.explanation: The passage says later writers learned that a novel could be built around a woman's inner life, that landscape could carry emotion, and that passion need not be polite to be true.

items.question: The phrase 'played with adult seriousness' in the passage suggests that the sisters':
options: Childhood games were taken as seriously as adult work
Novels were as intense and committed as their childhood inventions
Their books were meant for children
items.explanation: The passage compares their novels to a child's secret game played with adult seriousness, meaning the novels carry the same intensity as their childhood inventions but with mature commitment.

items.passage: For centuries, wetlands were treated as wasteland: damp, mosquito-ridden ground that was useful only when drained and built upon. Cities filled them in for housing, farmers drained them for fields, and engineers straightened the rivers that fed them. Only in recent decades have scientists and planners begun to understand what was lost. A wetland is not empty land waiting for a better use; it is one of the hardest-working ecosystems on the planet, and its services are worth far more than the buildings that replace it. The most valuable service a wetland provides is flood control. Like a sponge, it absorbs rainwater and river overflow, holds it, and releases it slowly. A single hectare of wetland can store thousands of cubic metres of water that would otherwise rush downstream and flood homes and roads. When the city of Chennai was hit by devastating floods in 2015, researchers pointed to the loss of its wetlands as a major cause: the city had paved over the very land that once soaked up the rain. Wetlands also clean water. As water passes slowly through reeds and mud, sediments settle, nutrients are absorbed by plants, and many pollutants break down. Towns that protect their wetlands spend less on water treatment, because nature does part of the work for free. They are also nurseries for life. Fish spawn in the shallow, sheltered waters, birds stop there on long migrations, and a huge variety of plants and insects thrive in the meeting of land and water. Nearly half of the world's threatened species depend on wetlands at some stage of their lives, which makes these habitats far more important than their small share of the earth's surface suggests. Beyond ecology, wetlands support livelihoods. Fisherfolk, reed cutters, and farmers who grow rice in the wet margins all depend on them, and in many parts of Asia and Africa the wetland is the centre of the local economy. Tourism adds another income: birdwatchers and nature lovers travel long distances to visit famous wetlands, bringing money to nearby villages. Despite all this, wetlands are disappearing three times faster than forests. The Ramsar Convention, an international treaty signed in 1971, now lists more than two thousand wetlands of international importance, but listing alone does not protect them. Enforcement is weak, and the pressure to drain land for agriculture and construction remains strong in fast-growing countries. Climate change makes the loss more dangerous. As rainfall becomes heavier and less predictable, the flood-absorbing capacity of wetlands matters more, not less. At the same time, rising seas threaten coastal wetlands with salt water, and hotter summers dry out inland marshes. The answer is not to fence off every wetland but to manage them wisely: restore the ones that have been damaged, keep new construction away from the most sensitive areas, and pay local people for protecting them rather than for draining them. Some cities have begun to do this, turning old wetlands into parks that absorb floods and give residents green space at the same time. The lesson is simple: a wetland is not a waste of land, it is a piece of infrastructure, and like any infrastructure it works best when it is maintained.
items.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Wetlands are valuable ecosystems that provide flood control, clean water and livelihoods
Wetlands are wastelands that should be drained for farming
Forests are more important than wetlands
Chennai's floods were caused only by heavy rain
The Ramsar Convention has solved the problem of wetland loss
items.explanation: The passage argues throughout that wetlands are hard-working ecosystems providing flood control, water cleaning, wildlife habitat and livelihoods, which the first option captures.

items.question: How does a wetland control floods, according to the passage?
options: By absorbing water like a sponge and releasing it slowly
By diverting rivers into the sea
By evaporating all the rainwater at once
By blocking the flow of rivers completely
items.explanation: The passage compares a wetland to a sponge that absorbs rainwater and river overflow, holds it, and releases it slowly, preventing sudden downstream flooding.

items.question: What role did the loss of wetlands play in the Chennai floods of 2015?
options: It was a major cause, as the city had paved over land that once soaked up rain
It had no role at all
It reduced the floods by half
It was the only cause of the floods
It helped the city recover faster
items.explanation: The passage says researchers pointed to the loss of Chennai's wetlands as a major cause, since the city had paved over the land that once soaked up the rain.

items.question: According to the passage, how do wetlands clean water?
options: By adding chemicals to the water
By filtering water through reeds and mud so sediments settle and pollutants break down
By boiling the water in the sun
By pumping water into treatment plants
By stopping all water from flowing
items.explanation: The passage explains that as water passes slowly through reeds and mud, sediments settle, nutrients are absorbed by plants, and many pollutants break down.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of wetlands?
items.explanation: The passage mentions flood control, wildlife nurseries, livelihoods and lower water treatment costs, but it never mentions electricity production from wetlands.

items.question: What does the passage say about the rate at which wetlands are disappearing?
options: They are disappearing three times faster than forests
They are disappearing at the same rate as forests
They are growing back faster than they are lost
They are disappearing only in Asia
items.explanation: The passage states plainly that wetlands are disappearing three times faster than forests, despite the Ramsar Convention's efforts.

items.question: Why does climate change make wetland loss more dangerous?
options: Because rainfall becomes heavier and less predictable, so flood absorption matters more
Because hotter summers make wetlands grow faster
Because rising seas create new wetlands
Because climate change has no effect on wetlands
items.explanation: The passage says heavier and less predictable rainfall makes the flood-absorbing capacity of wetlands matter more, not less, so losing them is more dangerous.

items.question: What solution does the author suggest for protecting wetlands?
options: Restore damaged wetlands, keep construction away from sensitive areas, and pay locals to protect them
Drain all wetlands and build treatment plants
Move all wetlands to national parks
items.explanation: The author says the answer is to restore damaged wetlands, keep construction away from sensitive areas, and pay local people for protecting them rather than draining them.

items.question: The author calls a wetland 'a piece of infrastructure' to suggest that:
options: Wetlands should be built by engineers
Wetlands perform a useful public service and work best when maintained
Wetlands are made of concrete and steel
Wetlands should be replaced by dams
Wetlands are only useful in cities
items.explanation: Calling a wetland infrastructure means it provides a public service like roads or drains, and like any infrastructure it works best when maintained rather than neglected.

items.passage: When Eleanor Roosevelt arrived at the United Nations in 1946, few expected her to achieve much. She had been the First Lady of the United States, but she had never held elected office, and the diplomats around the table were mostly men who doubted that a widow in her sixties could lead them. Within two years she had proved them wrong by guiding the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, a document that still shapes the way the world talks about freedom and dignity. Roosevelt's strength was not legal scholarship but persistence and common sense. She chaired a committee of eighteen people from different countries, cultures and political systems, and she kept them working through disagreements that often seemed impossible to resolve. When the Soviet delegates insisted that economic rights mattered more than political freedoms, and the Western delegates argued the opposite, she found language that allowed both sides to sign. She worked late into the night, read every draft herself, and refused to let the committee adjourn until the text was finished. Her approach to human rights was practical rather than abstract. She had visited slums and coal mines, met refugees and soldiers, and she believed that rights meant little unless they changed daily life. The Declaration she helped write therefore speaks of food, housing, education and work alongside freedom of speech and belief, because she knew that a hungry person cannot enjoy liberty. After the Declaration was adopted in December 1948, Roosevelt continued to fight for it, travelling the world to explain it and defending it against those who called it unrealistic. She once said that human rights begin in small places, close to home: in the neighbourhood, the school, the factory and the farm. Roosevelt's own life had taught her what hardship meant. Orphaned before she was ten, she was raised by a strict grandmother and sent to school in England, where a French headmistress, Marie Souvestre, encouraged her to think for herself and to care about the poor. Those years shaped the reformer she became, and she never forgot the loneliness of her childhood or the kindness of the teacher who believed in her. After the White House years she did not retire. She wrote a daily newspaper column, My Day, for more than twenty-five years, answering readers' letters and reporting on the places she visited. She supported the civil rights movement in America, resigned from organisations that refused black members, and used her fame to give a hearing to people who had none. In her seventies she was still travelling, still chairing committees, and still insisting that the work of rights was never finished. Unless rights have meaning there, she argued, they have little meaning anywhere. That belief guided everything she did, from the committee room in New York to the villages she visited on her travels. Her legacy is not only the document itself but the idea that ordinary people, not only lawyers and diplomats, own the language of rights and can use it to demand better lives.
items.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Eleanor Roosevelt guided the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights through persistence and practical sense
Eleanor Roosevelt was the first woman to hold elected office in the US
The United Nations was founded by Eleanor Roosevelt
Human rights are only about freedom of speech
The Soviet Union wrote the Universal Declaration
items.explanation: The passage focuses on how Roosevelt led the drafting of the Declaration through persistence, common sense and practical experience, which the first option sums up.

items.question: According to the passage, what was Roosevelt's main strength in the committee?
options: Her ability to speak many languages
items.explanation: The passage states plainly that her strength was not legal scholarship but persistence and common sense.

items.question: Why did the Declaration include food, housing, education and work?
options: Because Roosevelt knew a hungry person cannot enjoy liberty
Because the Soviet delegates demanded it alone
Because the Western delegates insisted on it
Because the document was about economics only
Because Roosevelt had never visited slums
items.explanation: The passage says she believed rights meant little unless they changed daily life, and she knew a hungry person cannot enjoy liberty, so the Declaration covers material needs too.

items.question: What did Roosevelt mean by saying human rights begin in small places?
options: Rights matter only in small towns
Rights must have meaning in daily life, in neighbourhoods, schools and workplaces
The United Nations should work only in villages
Human rights are unimportant at the global level
Only ordinary people need human rights
items.explanation: She argued that unless rights have meaning close to home, in the neighbourhood, school, factory and farm, they have little meaning anywhere, which is what the second option states.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Roosevelt chaired a committee of eighteen people
The Declaration was adopted in December 1948
Roosevelt had held elected office before joining the UN
Roosevelt worked late into the night on the drafts
Roosevelt defended the Declaration against critics
items.explanation: The passage says she had never held elected office before the UN, so the third statement is false. The other four are all stated in the passage.

items.question: A shop offers a 15% discount on a shirt priced at Rs. 240. What is the discount in rupees?
items.explanation: 15 percent of 240 is 0.15 times 240, which equals 36. So the discount is Rs. 36.

items.question: A man buys an article for Rs. 800 and sells it for Rs. 920. What is his profit percentage?
items.explanation: The profit is 920 minus 800, which is Rs. 120. As a percentage of the cost price 800, that is 120 divided by 800 times 100, which is 15 percent.

items.question: The ratio of two numbers is 3:5 and their sum is 64. What is the smaller number?
items.explanation: The two numbers are 3 parts and 5 parts of 64, so one part is 64 divided by 8, which is 8. The smaller number is 3 parts, which is 24.

items.question: A can do a job in 12 days and B can do it in 18 days. Working together, in how many days will they finish the job?
items.explanation: A does one twelfth of the job per day and B does one eighteenth, so together they do 5 thirty-sixths per day. The whole job therefore takes 36 divided by 5, which is 7.2 days.

items.question: A train 200 metres long crosses a pole in 10 seconds. What is its speed in km/h?
items.explanation: The train covers 200 metres in 10 seconds, which is 20 metres per second. Multiplying by 18 fifths to convert to km/h gives 72 km/h.
items.topic: Quantitative Aptitude - Time Speed and Distance

items.question: What is the simple interest on Rs. 5000 at 8% per annum for 3 years?
items.explanation: Simple interest is principal times rate times time divided by 100, which is 5000 times 8 times 3 divided by 100, giving Rs. 1200.

items.question: What is the compound interest on Rs. 10000 at 10% per annum compounded annually for 2 years?
items.explanation: The amount after two years is 10000 times 1.1 squared, which is Rs. 12100. The interest is 12100 minus 10000, which is Rs. 2100.

items.question: A number is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. What is the net percentage change?
items.explanation: A 20 percent rise followed by a 20 percent fall gives a net change of minus 20 times 20 divided by 100, which is minus 4 percent. The final value is 96 percent of the original.

items.question: A shopkeeper sells an article at a loss of 10%. If he had sold it for Rs. 90 more, he would have gained 5%. What is the cost price of the article?
items.explanation: Let the cost price be x. The two selling prices are 0.9x and 1.05x, and their difference is 90, so 0.15x equals 90 and x equals 600.

items.question: In what ratio must water be mixed with milk costing Rs. 40 per litre so that the mixture costs Rs. 32 per litre?
items.explanation: By alligation, the ratio of milk to water is 32 minus 0 to 40 minus 32, which is 32 to 8, or 4 to 1. So water to milk is 1 to 4.

items.question: If 3x + 5 = 2x + 12, what is the value of x?
items.explanation: Subtracting 2x from both sides gives x plus 5 equals 12, so x equals 7.

items.question: What is the sum of the roots of the equation x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0?
items.explanation: The equation factors as x minus 2 times x minus 3 equals zero, so the roots are 2 and 3, and their sum is 5. This also follows from the rule that the sum of the roots is minus the coefficient of x.

items.question: What is the sum of the first 10 terms of the arithmetic progression 2, 5, 8, ...?
items.explanation: The first term is 2 and the common difference is 3. The sum of 10 terms is 5 times twice 2 plus 9 times 3, which is 5 times 31, giving 155.

items.question: The sum of an infinite geometric progression is 12 and its first term is 8. What is the common ratio?
items.explanation: The sum of an infinite GP is the first term divided by one minus the ratio, so 12 equals 8 divided by one minus r. That gives one minus r equal to two thirds, so r equals one third.

items.question: What is the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 8 cm?
items.explanation: The area of a triangle is half the base times the height, which is half of 10 times 8, giving 40 square cm.

items.question: What is the area of a circle of radius 7 cm? (Take pi = 22/7)
items.explanation: The area is pi times radius squared, which is 22 sevenths times 49, giving 154 square cm.

items.question: What is the perimeter of a rectangle of length 12 cm and breadth 8 cm?
items.explanation: The perimeter is twice the length plus breadth, which is twice 20, giving 40 cm.

items.question: What is the volume of a cube of side 5 cm?
items.explanation: The volume of a cube is the side cubed, which is 5 cubed, giving 125 cubic cm.

items.question: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2:3:4. What is the largest angle?
items.explanation: The angles sum to 180 degrees, so one part is 180 divided by 9, which is 20 degrees. The largest angle is 4 parts, which is 80 degrees.

items.question: What is the HCF of 48 and 72?
items.explanation: The factors of 48 include 24 and the factors of 72 include 24, and no larger number divides both, so the HCF is 24.

items.question: Which of the following numbers is divisible by 9?
items.explanation: A number is divisible by 9 if its digit sum is divisible by 9. Only 12348 has a digit sum of 18, which is divisible by 9; the others have digit sums 15, 20, 25 and 30.

items.question: What is the remainder when 7^3 is divided by 5?
items.explanation: 7 cubed is 343, and 343 divided by 5 gives 68 with a remainder of 3.

items.question: How many factors does 72 have?
items.explanation: 72 equals 2 cubed times 3 squared, so the number of factors is 3 plus 1 times 2 plus 1, which is 4 times 3, giving 12.

items.question: A die is thrown once. What is the probability of getting an even number?
items.explanation: The even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6, which are 3 of the 6 equally likely outcomes, so the probability is 3 sixths, which is one half.

items.question: Two dice are thrown together. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
items.explanation: The pairs giving a sum of 7 are 1-6, 2-5, 3-4, 4-3, 5-2 and 6-1, which are 6 of the 36 equally likely outcomes, so the probability is 6 thirty-sixths, which is one sixth.

items.question: In how many ways can 3 people be chosen from a group of 6 people?
items.explanation: The number of combinations of 3 from 6 is 6 factorial divided by 3 factorial times 3 factorial, which is 720 divided by 36, giving 20.

items.question: In a group of 100 people, 60 like tea, 50 like coffee, and 20 like both. How many like neither?
items.explanation: The number who like at least one is 60 plus 50 minus 20, which is 90. So the number who like neither is 100 minus 90, which is 10.

items.question: What is the value of (sqrt(5) + sqrt(3)) x (sqrt(5) - sqrt(3))?
items.explanation: This is the difference of squares: the square of root 5 minus the square of root 3, which is 5 minus 3, giving 2.

items.question: What is the value of sin 30 degrees?
items.explanation: The sine of 30 degrees is a standard value, one half, which is 0.5.

items.question: A tower casts a shadow of 30 x sqrt(3) metres when the angle of elevation of the sun is 30 degrees. What is the height of the tower?
items.explanation: The height equals the shadow length times tan 30 degrees, which is 30 root 3 times one over root 3, giving 30 metres.

items.question: What is the value of x? Statement I: 2x + 3 = 11. Statement II: x is a positive integer.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives 2x equals 8, so x equals 4. Statement II alone only says x is positive, which does not fix its value. So statement I alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is Ram's present age? Statement I: Ram is 5 years older than Shyam. Statement II: Shyam is 20 years old.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives only the age difference, and statement II alone gives only Shyam's age. Together they give Ram's age as 20 plus 5, which is 25. So both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: Is A the brother of B? Statement I: A is the son of C. Statement II: B is the daughter of D.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: The statements give no link between C and D, so we cannot tell whether A and B belong to the same family at all. Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient.

items.question: What is the volume of a cuboid? Statement I: Its length is 5 cm and its breadth is 4 cm. Statement II: Its height is 3 cm.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Volume needs length, breadth and height. Statement I gives two of them and statement II gives the third, so together they give 5 times 4 times 3, which is 60 cubic cm. Both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: What is the profit percentage on an article? Statement I: The cost price is Rs. 400. Statement II: The selling price is Rs. 460.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Profit percentage needs both the cost price and the selling price. Statement I gives only the cost and statement II gives only the selling price, so both together are needed to find the profit of Rs. 60 on Rs. 400, which is 15 percent.

items.question: What is the average of x and y? Statement I: x + y = 100. Statement II: x = 60 and y = 40.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives the sum 100, so the average is 50. Statement II alone gives both values, so the average is also 50. Either statement alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the correct time now? Statement I: The clock shows 3:00 but it is 20 minutes fast. Statement II: The clock was set right at noon today.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone tells us the clock is 20 minutes fast, so the correct time is 2:40. Statement II alone gives no information about the current reading. So statement I alone is sufficient.

items.question: On which day of the week was 15 August 2024? Statement I: 1 August 2024 was a Thursday. Statement II: 2024 is a leap year.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: 15 August is exactly 14 days after 1 August, which is two whole weeks, so it falls on the same weekday, Thursday. Statement I alone is sufficient, and the leap year fact is irrelevant.

items.question: How many students play both cricket and football? Statement I: 60 play cricket and 50 play football. Statement II: There are 100 students in all and 10 play neither game.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: From statement II, 90 students play at least one game. Adding the two game counts gives 110, so the overlap is 110 minus 90, which is 20. Both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: What percentage of people like both tea and coffee? Statement I: 60% like tea and 50% like coffee. Statement II: 10% like neither tea nor coffee.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: From statement II, 90 percent like at least one. Adding 60 and 50 gives 110, so the overlap is 110 minus 90, which is 20 percent. Both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: What is the area of a rectangle? Statement I: Its length is twice its breadth. Statement II: Its perimeter is 36 cm.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives only the ratio of the sides, and statement II alone gives only their sum. Together, length plus breadth is 18 and length is twice breadth, so breadth is 6 and length is 12, giving an area of 72 square cm.

items.question: What is the radius of a circle? Statement I: Its circumference is 44 cm. Statement II: Its area is 154 square cm.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives the radius as 44 divided by 2 pi, which is 7 cm. Statement II alone gives the radius from pi r squared equals 154, which is also 7 cm. Either statement alone is sufficient.

items.question: Is x divisible by 6? Statement I: x is divisible by 2. Statement II: x is divisible by both 2 and 3.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Divisibility by 2 alone does not guarantee divisibility by 6, but divisibility by both 2 and 3 does, since 6 is 2 times 3 with coprime factors. So statement II alone is sufficient.

items.question: Is x an even number? Statement I: x^2 is an even number. Statement II: x is a multiple of 4.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: If x squared is even then x must be even, since the square of an odd number is odd. A multiple of 4 is also even. So either statement alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the speed of the train? Statement I: It covers 240 km in 4 hours. Statement II: It crosses a pole in 10 seconds.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives the speed as 240 divided by 4, which is 60 km/h. Statement II alone gives only the time to cross a pole, with no length, so it cannot give the speed. So statement I alone is sufficient.

items.question: What were the total sales of the company in the first quarter (January to March)?

diagram.caption: Monthly sales of a company (in Rs. lakh), January to June

items.explanation: The sales were 120 in January, 150 in February and 180 in March, and their sum is 450 lakh rupees.

items.question: In which month were the sales the highest?
items.explanation: The bar for May reaches 200 lakh rupees, which is higher than every other month shown in the chart.

items.question: By what percentage did sales increase from January to February?
items.explanation: Sales rose from 120 to 150, an increase of 30. As a percentage of 120, that is 30 divided by 120 times 100, which is 25 percent.

items.question: What was the average monthly sales over the six months?
items.explanation: The six monthly sales add up to 960 lakh rupees, and 960 divided by 6 is 160 lakh rupees per month.

items.question: Sales in May exceeded sales in April by what percentage?
items.explanation: Sales rose from 140 in April to 200 in May, an increase of 60. As a percentage of 140, that is 60 divided by 140 times 100, which is about 42.9 percent.

items.question: How many students were enrolled in all four departments together in 2023?

diagram.caption: Students enrolled in four departments, 2021 to 2023

items.explanation: In 2023 the enrolments were 180 in CS, 130 in EC, 120 in ME and 100 in CE, and their sum is 530.

items.question: Which department had the largest numerical growth in enrolment from 2021 to 2023?
items.explanation: CS grew from 120 to 180, a rise of 60, while EC, ME and CE each grew by exactly 40. So CS had the largest growth.

items.question: What was the percentage growth in EC enrolment from 2021 to 2023?
items.explanation: EC enrolment rose from 90 to 130, an increase of 40. As a percentage of 90, that is 40 divided by 90 times 100, which is about 44.4 percent.

items.question: How many students were enrolled in all four departments together in 2022?
items.explanation: In 2022 the enrolments were 150 in CS, 110 in EC, 100 in ME and 80 in CE, and their sum is 440.

items.question: What percentage of all students enrolled in 2023 were in the CS department?
items.explanation: CS had 180 of the 530 students enrolled in 2023, and 180 divided by 530 times 100 is about 34 percent.

items.question: In which year was the profit the lowest?

diagram.caption: Annual profit of a company (in Rs. crore), 2019 to 2023

items.explanation: The line dips to 18 crore rupees in 2021, which is lower than the profit in every other year shown.

items.question: What was the total profit of the company over the five years?
items.explanation: The yearly profits were 20, 25, 18, 30 and 35 crore rupees, and their sum is 128 crore rupees.

items.question: By what percentage did the profit increase from 2021 to 2022?
items.explanation: Profit rose from 18 to 30, an increase of 12. As a percentage of 18, that is 12 divided by 18 times 100, which is about 66.7 percent.

items.question: What was the average annual profit over the five years?
items.explanation: The total profit was 128 crore rupees over five years, and 128 divided by 5 is 25.6 crore rupees per year.

items.question: The profit in 2023 was what percentage more than the profit in 2019?
items.explanation: Profit rose from 20 in 2019 to 35 in 2023, an increase of 15. As a percentage of 20, that is 15 divided by 20 times 100, which is 75 percent.
